article.title: So, how did the polls do in 2024? It’s complicated
article.subtitle: By one important measure, they performed better than ever. By another, they had their worst year yet.

extraction.summary: Silver Bulletin's 2024 polling report card, published alongside its updated pollster ratings. In the 2023-24 cycle, average absolute polling error in the final 21 days was 4.5 points, the lowest in the database going back to 1998. Statistical bias, however, was D+2.9 points, the third straight presidential cycle in which the polls overestimated Democrats, and call accuracy was 70%, the lowest on record. The article describes the evaluation methodology: a 21-day window based on median field date, weighting each poll by 1/sqrt of its pollster's poll count, banned pollsters excluded, Advanced Plus-Minus, and half-credit for ties. It argues that herding and correlated bias make systematic error the key risk that probabilistic models must account for. It also reports historical call accuracy by poll margin and pollster-specific 2024 results, including AtlasIntel being upgraded to A+.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin defines polling error as the absolute difference between a poll's margin and the actual election margin between the top two candidates.
findings.model_version: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings / report card
findings.evidence_quote: By error, we mean the difference between a poll's margin and the actual margin of the election between the top two candidates.

findings.statement: The pollster ratings database used for accuracy evaluation covers polls since 1998 conducted in the final three weeks (21 days) before general elections for president, governor, Senate and House, and before presidential primaries.
findings.evidence_quote: our database since 1998, which covers polls in the final three weeks before general elections for president, governor, and Congress — and presidential primaries

findings.statement: Whether a poll falls inside the 21-day cutoff is determined by the poll's median field date.
Polls from pollsters banned by Silver Bulletin are excluded from the accuracy and bias analyses.

In aggregate accuracy statistics, each poll is weighted by 1/sqrt(N), where N is the number of polls its pollster conducted for that type of election in that cycle. This keeps prolific firms from dominating the averages.

quantities.name: weight
quantities.context: N = polls by pollster for race type in cycle

findings.rationale: To avoid giving prolific polling firms too much influence.
findings.model_version: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings / report card
findings.evidence_quote: weighted by one over the square root of the number of polls that their pollster conducted for that particular type of election in that particular cycle

findings.statement: Odd-numbered years are grouped with the following even-numbered year into two-year cycles (for example, 2023-2024) for evaluation.
findings.rationale: Odd years have few qualifying polls, only off-cycle gubernatorial races and special elections.
findings.evidence_quote: We group odd-numbered years (e.g., 2023) together with even-numbered ones (2024) because there aren't many qualifying polls in these

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin applies specific inclusion rules to presidential primary polls. Because almost none of the few 2024 Democratic primary polls met these rules, the database contains no 2024 Democratic primary polls.
findings.evidence_quote: basically none of them followed the various rules we apply to primary polls — there are no 2024 Democratic primary polls in our database anyway

findings.statement: The weighted-average absolute polling error across all race types since 1998 is 5.9 points. By race type it is: presidential primary 9.1, presidential general 4.2, Senate 5.4, House 6.0, governor 5.4.

In the 2023-24 cycle, average absolute polling error was 4.5 points, the lowest of any cycle since 1998. By race type it was: presidential general 3.4 (second-lowest on record), Senate 4.1 (lowest on record), House 5.2, governor 5.4, presidential primary 9.8.
findings.evidence_quote: in 2023-2024, the average polling error was lower than in any cycle in our database at only 4.5 points

findings.statement: Presidential primary polls have by far the largest error of any race type, for two reasons. First, multicandidate fields mean voters who like several options switch late or vote tactically for candidates who seem likely to finish strongly. Second, low turnout makes it hard to predict who will vote.
findings.evidence_quote: presidential primaries usually feature multiple candidates... Second, presidential primaries feature much lower turnout than general elections.

findings.statement: The 2024 cycle's low average error was partly an artifact of composition. There were few presidential primary polls, which are the highest-error type, so their absence pulled the combined average down.
findings.evidence_quote: primary polls also tend to have the largest polling error... so their relative absence this cycle helped pull down the average error

findings.statement: Pollster herding, meaning reluctance to publish outliers, can improve individual firms' measured accuracy. It reduces the benefit of averaging because the polls carry redundant information, so an average of herded polls is less informative than the number of polls suggests.
findings.evidence_quote: Herding may yield stronger performance for individual polling firms but reduces the benefit of averaging or aggregation since the polls are all basically telling you the same thing.

findings.statement: Because polls tend to err in the same direction, averaging does little to reduce systematic bias. Forecast models must therefore explicitly account for systematic (correlated) polling error. This is an advantage of probabilistic models over simple polling averages.
findings.rationale: Averaging doesn't help when almost all polls are off in the same direction.
findings.model_version: general principle / Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model
findings.evidence_quote: it's more important than ever to account for the possibility of a systematic polling error. Because probabilistic election models do this, that's one advantage they have over simple polling averages

findings.statement: In the 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential model, the single most likely outcome was Trump sweeping all seven swing states, and the next-most likely was Harris sweeping all seven. This reflects strong correlation of errors between states in the simulations.
findings.evidence_quote: Trump sweeping all seven closely contested swing states was the most likely outcome in our model

findings.statement: Statistical bias is the signed average error, i.e. how far polls consistently underestimate one party. It is calculated only for races where the top two finishers were a Democrat and a Republican, so it is not computed for presidential primaries.
findings.evidence_quote: statistical bias: the extent to which polls miss in the same direction and consistently underestimate Democrats or Republicans

findings.statement: Historically, the direction of polling bias has been unpredictable from cycle to cycle. For example, polls underestimated Democrats in 2012 and Republicans in 2014 and 2016.
findings.evidence_quote: Historically, the direction of bias has been unpredictable cycle-to-cycle.

findings.statement: Polls overestimated Democrats in three consecutive presidential elections. Combined bias was D+3.0 in 2016 (described as about 3 points), D+4.7 in 2020 and D+2.9 in 2024. Presidential-only bias was D+3.2 in 2016, D+4.1 in 2020 and D+2.9 in 2024.
findings.evidence_quote: In 2016, the polls had a 3-point average bias toward Democrats. In 2020, bias was D+4.7 points. And this year, it was a smaller but still substantial at D +2.9.

findings.statement: In 2024, polling bias was highly consistent across race types: D+2.9 in presidential, Senate and House polls, and D+1.8 in gubernatorial polls. This is consistent with declining ticket-splitting, which implies polling errors are correlated across offices in presidential years.
findings.evidence_quote: With less and less ticket-splitting in presidential years, that's what you'd expect.

findings.statement: All-years average bias since 1998 is D+1.1 combined. By race type: president D+1.3, Senate D+0.7, House D+1.3, governor D+0.9. Midterm cycles show small bias: 2018 R+0.5 combined (Senate EVEN, House R+0.4, governor R+1.0) and 2022 D+0.8 combined (Senate R+0.3, House D+0.2, governor D+1.3).

The repeated Democratic bias may be Trump-specific, because bias was much lower in 2022 and slightly Republican in 2018 when Trump was not on the ballot. If so, 2026 and 2028 polls might not show the same bias. Pollsters Silver Bulletin spoke with were mixed on this.
findings.evidence_quote: It could, for example, be a Trump-specific issue.

findings.statement: Call accuracy (whether the poll leader won) is a poor measure of poll accuracy and serves only as a sanity check. A poll showing Trump +1 in a state he won by 13 is still a bad result, while a poll showing Trump +1 when Harris won by 1 would be pretty good.
findings.rationale: Magnitude of error matters, not just direction.
findings.evidence_quote: we've never thought of this as a great way to assess how accurate the polls are

findings.statement: In call-accuracy scoring, a pollster gets half-credit if its poll shows a tie for the lead and one of the tied candidates wins.

Polls have called the correct winner 77.8% of the time since 1998 (about 78%). In 2024 the rate was 70.1%, the lowest on record. Presidential general election polls called 62.8% correctly, the worst since 1998. House polls called 65.6%, Senate 77.8%, governor 92.2% and presidential primary 97.3%.
findings.evidence_quote: Across all cycles since 1998, polls have predicted the correct winner 78 percent of the time. In 2024, call accuracy was only 70 percent

findings.statement: All-years call accuracy by race type: presidential primary 82.8%, presidential general 76.9%, Senate 80.8%, House 72.2%, governor 82.1%.

Historical call accuracy by the poll's margin: under 3 points 56.0%, 3-6 points 69.1%, 6-10 points 85.8%, 10-15 points 93.8%, 15-20 points 96.9%, 20 or more points 99.5%. This gives an empirical mapping from poll lead to win probability.
findings.evidence_quote: Historically, polls showing leads of less than 3 points call only 56 percent of races correctly — not much better than a coin flip.

findings.statement: Poll leads of less than 3 points tell you very little and should be treated as toss-ups. Polls are not precise enough to resolve them.
findings.evidence_quote: Please don't treat leads of less than 3 points as telling you very much at all.

findings.statement: Call accuracy depends heavily on how competitive the polled races are. 2024 primary polls scored high because the race was noncompetitive, and general election polls scored low because the race was close. Pollsters increasingly concentrate on competitive states, which lowers measured call accuracy.
findings.evidence_quote: it's a function of the races being polled in each case

findings.statement: Advanced Plus-Minus measures how a pollster's average error compares to other pollsters' error in the same election, with further statistical adjustments for race difficulty and sample size. Negative scores are better.
findings.evidence_quote: how the pollster's average error compares to other pollsters' in the same election, with various other statistical adjustments that account for which races are harder and easier to poll

findings.statement: The pollster ratings use each pollster's data back to 1998 and weight recent years more heavily.
findings.evidence_quote: our pollster ratings weight recent years more heavily

findings.statement: A pollster's single-cycle performance should not be overweighted. The multi-cycle ratings are better for judging quality, although 2024 shifted the ratings more than most cycles do.
findings.evidence_quote: You shouldn't put too much stock in a pollster's performance in a single cycle

findings.statement: After 2024, AtlasIntel was upgraded from A to A+ and became the highest-rated pollster in the database, and OnMessage moved from B/C to A. Selzer kept a B+ despite 12.8 points of average error and D+14.8 bias in 2023-24.
findings.evidence_quote: AtlasIntel's rating has gone from an A to an A+ — and it is now the highest-rated pollster in our database — while OnMessage moved from a B/C to an A

findings.statement: 2023-24 pollster results, for pollsters with at least 5 polls in the final 21 days (given as error / bias / APM / number of polls): OnMessage 1.2 / D+0.1 / -2.2 / 20; Patriot Polling 1.5 / D+1.5 / -1.2 / 15; AtlasIntel 1.5 / D+0.1 / -1.2 / 67; Mitchell 2.0 / D+1.2 / -1.5 / 6; Echelon 2.0 / D+0.3 / -0.9 / 8; TIPP 2.0 / D+2.0 / -1.3 / 22; Washington Post 2.0 / D+1.8 / -1.4 / 8; Beacon/Shaw 2.1 / D+2.1 / -0.9 / 6; InsiderAdvantage 2.2 / D+1.1 / -1.5 / 25; Trafalgar 2.5 / D+1.0 / -1.3 / 29; Rasmussen 2.7 / D+0.4 / -0.9 / 25; Redfield & Wilton 2.8 / D+2.4 / -0.5 / 36; Quinnipiac 2.8 / D+2.8 / -0.0 / 6; Susquehanna 2.9 / D+1.1 / -0.9 / 6; PPP 2.9 / R+2.1 / -3.7 / 6; Saint Anselm 2.9 / D+2.4 / -2.4 / 5; Monmouth 3.1 / D+1.8 / -1.3 / 8; Emerson 3.3 / D+1.9 / -1.5 / 61; J.L. Partners 3.5 / R+0.7 / -1.3 / 8; Marist 3.5 / D+3.4 / 0.7 / 13; SSRS 3.6 / D+3.6 / 0.5 / 15; OH Predictive 3.7 / D+3.7 / -1.3 / 10; NYT/Siena 3.9 / D+3.9 / 0.4 / 21; Focaldata 3.9 / D+3.9 / 0.5 / 9; Data for Progress 4.0 / D+3.2 / 0.7 / 8.

In 2024, pollsters with Democratic-leaning house effects (such as YouGov) performed worse and those with Republican-leaning house effects performed better. Siena, SurveyUSA and YouGov had biases of about D+5.
findings.evidence_quote: firms like YouGov that had Democratic-leaning house effects performed worse, while those with R-leaning ones were better

findings.statement: Historical track records matter, but relying on them can be overdone. No single poll should be treated as an oracular gold standard, because previously accurate firms can have bad cycles and newer firms can outperform.
findings.evidence_quote: it's a bad idea to treat one poll as an oracular gold standard

findings.statement: Generic ballot polls, which ask about the Democrat or Republican House candidate without naming them, are counted toward House poll accuracy ratings. Selzer's district-level House polls used this format and were also counted.
findings.evidence_quote: this is the same format that most generic ballot polls use... and we count those toward our accuracy ratings

findings.statement: The Advanced Plus-Minus statistic accounts for poll sample size.
findings.evidence_quote: These polls also had small sample sizes, but our Advanced Plus-Minus stat accounts for that.

political_insights.insight: With less ticket-splitting in presidential years, polling bias is nearly identical across presidential, Senate and House races.
political_insights.evidence: In 2024, bias was D+2.9 for president, Senate and House.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model polling errors as highly correlated across offices within a presidential year.

political_insights.insight: Polls underestimated Republicans when Trump was on the ballot (2016, 2020, 2024) but not in the 2018 and 2022 midterms.
political_insights.evidence: 2018 bias R+0.5 and 2022 bias D+0.8 combined, versus D+3.0, D+4.7 and D+2.9 in presidential years.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Consider whether to apply a prior on directional bias in future cycles without Trump on the ballot; the evidence is uncertain.

political_insights.insight: Trump's unpopularity is expected to carry electoral consequences for Republicans in 2025 special elections and the 2026 midterms.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Presidential approval feeds into midterm expectations.

political_insights.insight: Pollsters concentrate resources on competitive states and rarely poll safe states such as Alabama or Vermont.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Safe states have sparse polling, so fundamentals or priors matter more there.

open_questions: The exact formula for Advanced Plus-Minus, including how it adjusts for race difficulty and sample size.
The recency-weighting scheme used in the pollster ratings.
The specific inclusion rules for primary polls.
How pollster grades (A+, B+, etc.) map to the underlying scores.
How the 2024 presidential model parameterizes correlated state errors to produce the sweep outcomes.
